title: Shangani shopping street
text:
This alley, well known by business owners and tourists, rarely sees a quiet day. My attention is pulled between navigating and observing the movement of the street and the beautiful display of earrings to my left as well as the kind vender offering to let me try them in inside their store.

The street is loud, busy, acting as a shopping high street. Each darker frame, contrasting the sun lit facade represents the entrance into another shop or small business that stretches out into the street through displacs, clothes and product placed on the ground close to its entrance.

It almost becomes unnoticable that the buildings continue oast the ground floor where all activity and noise is concentrated. The more private ‘quiet actors’ pf the second, third and fourth floors remain hidden above eye sight and in the shade of the overhangs. These become ‘irrelevant’ to visitors and tourists, with only the occasional pop of colour such as this green, encouraging you to look up

title: Shangani alley way
text:
While most activity is contained within the ground floor, effecting the stream of movement, the tall facades contribute to the tight feeling of the streets, growing way above my head I almost feel as though I am walking indoors. 

The levels are divided up by sun shades attached to the facades, keeping much of the building hidden from me and framing my view of the sky above me. 

The tangled net of power cables are kept comfortably above me so that I never get into direct contact with them, they dangle from building to building creating interesting patterns that dissolbe into the background. 

My attention is typucally contain to what is immediatly infont of me, the slow moving sky offers a calming contrast to the fast paced and at times, overstimulating street.

Around me I hear chatting in Arabic, Swahili, German, English and French reflecting the diverse range of people attracted to Zanzibar, all trying to navigate these streets. Children are running past me and the honking of boda bodas (motorcycles) cues me to jump to the side as they travel through the alleyways that feel like they should be too small for these fast moving vehicles.

title: Shangani shopping
text:
“Although I remember many of these streets and where the paths leads to, moving around requires a certain confidence and ability to push aside the fear of getting lost; fully embracing ‘derive’. The colourful shops, occasional breeze, sound of chattering, motorcucles and bike bells, create a lively athmisphere. As I move my nose is hit with smells of dust, then spices (nutmeg, clove, cinnamon, stand out) and perfumes like jasmine and rose. 

The ground is uneven and a constant flow means little time is given to make a decision about the next turn or path to take. The decision is typically made for e as I begin to notice that I follow the light. Choosing the path that is best lit but the sun meaning my sense of direction is dictated by the time of day and location of the sun in the sky.

Above me a tangled net of electricity cables snakes from house to house showing how the city has been forced to adapt to the rapid growth. It covers up much of what used to be there before including old lamps and even street cameras.

title: Shangani church
text:
The narrow, winding alleyways always make me focus on what is ahead. You can never see more than what is a few steps in front o fyou and every turn is like a surprise. Some roads will squeese you even tighter while others offer slightly more breathing room. 

Though, here, my gaze started moving up. The tall walls and small shading devices frame snippets of the sky above, acting as a frame to the outside world, strictly controlling what can be seen and giing small hints to your location. Here, between the roofs, shutters and A/C boxes, the towers of the nearby church could be seen against a perfectly blue sky, the dark alleyway being a strong contrast to the light (sun catching) structure ahead. Like a picture inside a frame it could be seen clearly but not in its entirety; and the path towards it remains a myster that can only be uncovered by continuing the walk. In my case, unfortunetly, one wrong turn meant I lost sight of it.

title: Kiponda alley way
text:
The narrow pathways only reveil what is just a head of you. Planning your route is a near to impossible task and you have to let the winding street act as your guide, allowing the feeling of being lost to give way to exploration and anticipation. 

These paths are shared by shop keepers who typically sit on the sides, trying to convince you to enter and buy something. Tourists move in and out of countless of these stores. I am convinced they may not even know if they have been to the same place twice.

At the same time, school children are running past, motorcycles, bikes and large carts make their way past you. Stopping mid road is never a consideration, it is a consistent flow, though the pace may slow or increase depending on the road. The only ‘pause’ available is when seeking refuge in one of the stores on the side of the road. Here it is possible to stop, breath and break away from the moving stream outside.

title: Kiponda Golden Hour
text: The beautifully carved ‘Zanzibar doors’ are now one of the most recognised elements of Zanzibar and its history. They decorate the entrances to homes, portraying family and religious values. Yet they now alos act as the backdrop to countless tourist photos. Each door is hand carved and unique, though motives repeat, finding a replica is near impossible.

title: Kiponda Noon
text:
Not only the sun shining directly over our head but alos the sudden increase in temperature signals mid-day/ There is almost an eerie, unexpected quieteness, the slowing down of your pace in response to the pressing weather. The roof scape (overhangs and shades) are now almost reflected 1:1 on the floor as their shadows decorate the ground and reveal what is up above our heads. this is the brightes the little alleyways will be lit, the direct sun reveals new, previously hidden corners, and everything becomes visisble, even the power chords ceate interesting patters on the ground shwoing how the city continues to evolve and adapt. 

The only thing that remains in the dark are the windows. Mosquito nets covered in thick layers of dust keep what is behind these walls private. While the bright alleyways already steel our attention, the stark contrast to these dark entry points make the paths feel even more congested.

title: Kiponda Sunset
text:
Having walked into an open area, adjacent to the beach, the passing of the day is now documented by the long shados of the palm trees and passers by, decorating the facades of buildings. The athmosphere is filled with sounds as people are finishing their way days and instead are preparing for dinner, diving into the ocean, or are playing a large game of footbal.

The 5pm sun casts a warm golden glow over the facades, romanticising every crack and exposed brick. In the case of this unused (still not renovated) ocean facing house, the passing of time is beginning to expose the coral walls, an older construction technique that made us of locally available resources for architecture. Here each coral rock, unique in size and shape, is perfectly fitted between its neighbours, demonstrtaing a slow but extremely precise craft.

title: Spice Market
text:
The low hanging orange and red canvaes create a tight space that makes you feel like you need to keep your neck bent and gaze down towards the stall tables at all times. The shade, warm glow from the canopies above create not just a different athmosphere but almost an entirely new world or environment that I have now always associated with the purchasing of spices. Tables are laid out in a tight grid formation, allowing a maximum of two people to walk past at a time. You are easily pulled into conversation with venders as the strong smeel of cloves, cinamon, chili, cashews, cardamon, masala and chai navigate you through the space, a welcome change to the strong fish smells from the wet market just adjacent. 

While almost every store sells a combination of the same products everyone walks through eyeing each stall carefully. I am convinced it is less the products that make you stop and more a pause in the stream of movement through the grid. 

The overwhelming combination of various stimulants, including he red light, spot lights in the ceiling where the fabric or metal sheets have left a gap, venders promoting their product, smell of spices, uneven ground and tight spaces do not make this a space to linger. As son as I grabbed the opportunity of a pause I was also pulled into a transaction that I only left after having purches many incredible spices. Their smell in my bag stil brings me back to this site.

title: Stone Town Frames
text:
Fascinated by the way light and shadow guides movement throughout Stone Town, these kinds of alleyways catch my attention. The darker alley, wall walls act as a frame letting you peak through into the adjacent street. Never fully revealing what is there the ‘light at the end of the tunnel’ is often enough to pull me through, allowing my curiosity to guide my wander through the site. With each walk, at different times of the day, different alleyways get darker and other get highlighted, changing the circulation and movement through the city. 

A sturdy and consistent flow of movement guided by the light will keep you walking in a somewhat steady direction acting as your guide and sene of orientation within this confined space where connection to the ‘outside’ feels limited.

These windows are a defining characteristic of Stone Town, as I have walked these streets many times, the roof scapes, ground and doors becoming familar landscapes, some of these remain well known and allow me to wander with more confidence. 

In this particular case the dark alley would have led to a slightly larger open, public space just outside a religion school. It acts as a place of rest for anties and an opportunity of play for children.

title: Views Above
text:
Looking up towards the sky and ‘roof scape’ will never fail to reveal an interesting new detail. Though the view of the sky is often kept in strict frames, it does, on occasion peak through more, reflecting the open space I just walked into. While I don’t often look up as I fear tripping over a brick or dent in the floor, I always admire the rounded or petal shaped windows, carved wooden balconies and shadow play on the facades.

Almost reaching the noon sun, th glare and heat becomes close to unbearable, but the soft, salty breeze tells me I am not far from the beach, a place of refuge if I plan on escaping the tight roads where the heat will collect. 

The open space lets me slow down, take in th space and admire thetall facade growing next to me, making me wander what my view would be looking out from one of these windows.

title: Stone Town Shops
text:
The rhythmic humm of the fan greets me as I walk into this space. The shop with its high ceiling, low lighting and overall ‘stillness’ acts as a calming pause, in contrast to the constant movement in the crowded streets outside. 

My eyes have to adjust to the slighter darker room, lit by just tow lights hanging from the ceiling. My view is first pulled ack to the bright entrance revealing the sun lit street outside. Then the breeze of the fan, light movement of the hangng/displayed clothes and smell of this humid stone-and-wooden room pulls me back in. The calm athmosphere of the room invites me to browse and while no signs are put up, the staircase left in the dark immediately communicates privacy - a space off limits. Similarly to navigating the streets outside, here light guides your movement through the store.

title: View to the Outside
text:
The contrast shown here, points to the brightly, sun-lit street, busy street, which, compared to the subdued, darker, interior, always indicates the next path/route or destination. 

The heavy wooden doors seperating the inside from the outside caught my attention. Though not quiet as decorated as most Zanzibar doors, the pattern and impressive size demonstrates local craft and craftsmeship. While my gaze often moves towards the water stains on walls, cracks in stone, the tangled net of cables and darkening paint, this is an important reminder of the craft hidden within these spots, the reminders of tradition, local knowledge and art as well as how these spaces are constantly adapted and changed with the times, even as the rest of this UNESCO world heritage site appears almost locked in time.
